title: Tuples, named records, dictionaries and sets
outcome: Choose collection representations according to identity, ordering, mutability and lookup needs.
key_terms: An immutable, fixed-length ordered collection whose element types are part of its own type.
An immutable tuple with named fields, such as `(id = 7, score = 0.5)`, read with field syntax like `row.score`.
A hash table that maps keys to values and whose iteration order is unspecified, so reports should sort keys explicitly.
Dictionaries and sets match keys with `isequal` and `hash`, so `1` and `1.0` select the same entry.
An unordered collection of distinct elements that uses the same equality and hashing rules as dictionary keys.
approach: Pick each container for the question it answers. Tuples hold fixed positional fields, named tuples label them, a count dictionary keeps multiplicity that a `Set` drops, `haskey` separates absence from a stored zero, and dictionary keys follow `isequal`. Presentation order is imposed with `sort`, never inherited from hashing.

exercises.title: Make one tuple element
exercises.task: Represent a single integer as a tuple.
exercises.answer: The tuple syntax distinguishes a one-field collection from the scalar value.
exercises.why: `(7,)` is a one-element tuple; the trailing comma is what makes it a tuple, since `(7)` is just the integer 7.
exercises.wrong: Writing `(7)` and calling `length` returns 1 by accident for an integer, hiding that the value is not a collection.

exercises.title: Name a returned record
exercises.task: Return an ID, score and eligibility field.
exercises.expected: Callers can access fields by their names.
exercises.hint: Prefer explicit semantic labels to remembered positions.
exercises.answer: The representation makes a small fixed schema inspectable.
exercises.why: Returning `(id = 1, score = 0.8, eligible = true)` lets callers write `result.score` instead of remembering that score is second.
exercises.wrong: Returning a plain tuple and reading `result[2]` breaks silently if a field is later inserted before score.
exercises.verify: Access each field by name and assert `keys(result) == (:id, :score, :eligible)`.

exercises.title: Preserve multiplicity
exercises.task: Count the labels `a`, `b`, `b` before converting them to a set.
exercises.expected: Counts are 1 and 2 while the set has two distinct labels.
exercises.hint: Frequency and membership are different questions.
exercises.answer: Deduplication intentionally discards multiplicity and can change a scientific denominator.
exercises.why: Counting `a`, `b`, `b` gives `a => 1` and `b => 2`, while `Set(["a", "b", "b"])` keeps only two members.
exercises.wrong: Converting to a set first and then counting reports one of each label, which halves the weight of `b`.
exercises.verify: Assert the count dictionary has `b => 2` and `length(Set(labels)) == 2`.

exercises.title: Control presentation order
exercises.task: Print a dictionary in an explicitly sorted key order.
exercises.expected: The report follows the chosen ordering rule.
exercises.hint: Do not depend on traversal order.
exercises.answer: Stable presentation requires an explicit contract rather than an incidental implementation order.
exercises.why: Iterating `sort(collect(keys(d)))` gives a fixed order regardless of how the dictionary hashed its keys.
exercises.wrong: Printing `d` directly and pasting it into a report assumes insertion order, which `Dict` does not promise.
exercises.verify: Print the report twice with differently built dictionaries holding the same pairs and compare the transcripts.

exercises.title: Separate absent and zero
exercises.task: Compare a present zero-valued key with an absent key.
exercises.hint: A default value can conceal missingness.
exercises.answer: Only use an absent-to-zero convention when the measurement contract justifies it.
exercises.why: `Dict("a" => 0)` stores a real zero for `a`, while `b` is absent, so `haskey` gives true and false.
exercises.wrong: Reading with `get(values, key, 0)` reports both as 0 and loses the difference between measured zero and no record.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `haskey`, `get(values, "b", -1) == -1` and `@test_throws KeyError values["b"]`.

exercises.title: Inspect special keys
exercises.task: Use NaN and both signed zeros as dictionary keys.
exercises.expected: NaN is retrievable and the signed zeros remain distinct in this fixture.
exercises.answer: Dictionary equality semantics should match the application meaning of the keys.
exercises.why: Keys use `isequal`, so `NaN` finds itself and `0.0` and `-0.0` are different keys, leaving three entries.
exercises.wrong: Expecting `==` semantics predicts that NaN cannot be retrieved and that the signed zeros collapse into two entries.

checks_note: Lookup behavior differs by method. `haskey` asks without failing, `get` supplies the fallback -1, and direct indexing of a missing key raises `KeyError`, which is the right signal when the key must exist. The `special` dictionary uses `isequal` for keys, so NaN finds itself and `0.0` and `-0.0` stay separate entries, giving length 3. Code that compares keys with `==` would merge the zeros and lose NaN.
